title: Mu Alpha Theta
text:
Mu Alpha Theta is a national honor society in the United States for high school and two year college students. Mu Alpha Theta chapters host numerous mathematics competitions and each year a national Mu Alpha Theta convention is held during the summer.

Structure[edit]

(NOTE: The following format of competition refers only to the state and national level competitions. Many states, including Florida, Louisiana, and Mississippi have varying sets of regional competitions as well prior to these conventions).

Some States hold a State Convention each year in their capital city, which usually involves multiple days at a hotel or convention center. These conventions may offer more than just an Individual or Team Round. The Florida (FAMAT) State Convention offers sets of Topic Tests (Same style as individual tests but with a specific topic of focus) per division, as well as other rounds.

In the summer, the Mu Alpha Theta organization has a National Convention, hosted in a different city/state each year by a member school. The following types of tests are listed below.

The Tests[edit]

Individual[edit]

The test is a multiple choice test with 4 choices and an extra choice called NOTA, which means None Of The Above. Test topics usually follow school curriculum subjects; however they are far more advanced. The main groups in the regional and invitational levels are:

  • Algebra 1
  • Geometry
  • Algebra 2
  • Pre - Calculus
  • Statistics
  • Calculus

You are primarily involved in one of each division a year. The lowest division you can participate in is locked to the current class you are taking, but you can participate in higher divisions. You cannot stay in any division other than Calculus for more than one year.

At the national level, Alegbra 1 is removed, and the remaining divisions are regrouped and renamed as:

Mu - Calculus

Alpha - Precalculus

Theta - Geometry & Algebra 2 (Focus on Algebra 2)

The tests are often made by other students, or faculty at member schools.

Individual tests generally have 30 questions. There is also a one hour time limit except for History of Math which has a 30 minute time limit. The scoring system usually is as follows:

  • 5 points for each correct question
  • 1 points for each unanswered question
  • 0 for each incorrect question

Team Rounds[edit]

In team rounds, teams of the 4 best people from each school work fast to answer a set of 4 problems in 4 minutes. However, the faster a team turns in an answer, the more points received.

You receive 2 points for each part you answer correctly. However, depending on the minute in which you answer it, you may receive bonus points as follows, if you got all 4 parts correct:

  • Correct answer in first minute
    • +12 points
  • Correct answer in second minute
    • +8 points
  • Correct answer in third minute
    • +4 points
  • Correct answer in fourth minute
    • +0 points (No bonus points)

This round is NOT multiple choice.

This bonus is also considered a sliding bonus. That means, the first team to answer all 4 question right the earliest, will receive the full 12 points, and any team that answered in the same minute will also get 12 points. From that minute onwards, the scale goes down normally.

Questions, just as in the individual round, often follow a certain subject consistent by question.

Questions usually follow the certain format:

A=<insert some kind of math problem here>

B=<Insert some kind of math problem here>

C=<Insert some kind of math problem here>

D=<Insert some kind of math problem here>

However, this is not always the case.

There are usually 13 or 14 questions, but only the first 12 are scored unless a question is thrown out (more on that later). If one is thrown out, then the score from the 13th question is used, then the 14th if necessary.

Ciphering[edit]

The Ciphering Test is the third major test in the Mu Alpha Theta National Convention and the State Conventions.

The Ciphering Test is an individual-style test. It is a series of 10 or 12 questions on a small packet.

For each question, you are given 3 minutes to answer the problem. You receive the following points by minute for answering a question correctly:

  • Correct answer in first minute
    • +12 points
  • Correct answer in second minute
    • +8 points
  • Correct answer in third minute
    • +4 points

You will usually find that scores on this round are very low, because these tests are usually difficult with the time pressure.

The combined Individual and Ciphering score gives the Composite score, which is used to determine who in a school's competitor list will sit for the team round.

Topic Tests[edit]

For each of the three main divisions (Mu, Alpha, Theta), the MAO convention offers many different topic tests (8 to 9 per division). Here are the common ones:

Theta:


Equations & Inequalities

Functions

Logarithms & Exponents

Applications (Word Problems)

CPAV (Circumference, Perimeter, Area & Volume)

Geometry

Conic Sections

Sequence & Series

Quadrilaterals

Circles & Polygons


Alpha:


Trigonometry

Equations & Inequalities

Analytic Geometry

Applications

Matrices & Vectors

Complex Numbers

Sequences & Series

Polar & Parametric

Logarithms & Exponents


Mu:


Limits & Derivatives

Applications

Integration

BC Calculus

Sequences & Series

Area & Volume

Polar & Parametric

Additionally, there are Open tests, available to all divisions:

History of Mathematics

Number Theory

Discrete Math

Statistics Unplugged

Probability & Combinatorics

Codes & Ciphers

Comprehensive (Any topic from any division)

Any student can choose to take topic tests from a higher division.

Gemini[edit]

This is a normal Individual-style test, but it's questions are similar to that of the American Mathematics Competitions (AMC), but with calculus in the Mu division. Additionally, the test is taken in pairs. This test is separated by division, and only two students in each school from each division can take it.

It is usually held at the same time as the Team round, because non-team members are supposed to take this test.

Speed & Mental Math[edit]

This is another test separated by division, but only six students from each school from each division may take it (Three for Speed, Three for Mental). Only the best of the three can receive an award in either test.

Speed Math is 25 open response problems in 15 minutes. Mental Math is 40 open response problems in 8 minutes.

ANY scratch marks on your paper for Mental Math other than writing the answer results in disqualification, as does any erasing.

Sponsors (As in teachers and coaches) are allowed to take this test. They are ranked for awards separately from students.

Relay & Hustle[edit]

Relay is an individual test (3 participants per school per division). Hustle is a team test (4 members). No person can take both Relay and Hustle.

In relay, each round is 10 minutes, in which a 6-question set is given. The team members sit in an order dictated by the round rules, based on their division.

Each question succeeding the first relies on the answer of the previous question to solve it. This means getting any question wrong will mess up all other questions in the set.

You receive 5 points for any question answered correctly in a round. If any question is answered incorrectly, no more points may be given for any other question in that round.

There are 5 rounds.

In hustle, there are 5 rounds of 5 minutes.

125 questions are provided to each team, 25 from each division (Geo, Alg 2, Precal, Calculus, and Stats).

In the last one minute of each round, the team will compile all answered questions and give it to the judge. The points earned per question correct goes down by round (6, 5, 4, 3, 2 respectively).

Interschool[edit]

This is an interdivision test of various math trivia, puzzles, and logic.

Each school starts with one student answering problems, who can choose to either solve the normal problemset, or solve questions from a separate problemset in order to allow more students from their school to enter and help (known as "buying in").

In the last 15 minutes, all students are allowed in the testing room.

Poster[edit]

At the start of the convention, the topic of the poster is announced. Schools must make and design a poster by the final awards ceremony.

Chalk Talk[edit]

Students are asked to prepare a presentation (with only a 3x5 notecard) on a specifc topic per division. The first round is held online. 10 students from each division are announced as finalists a few weeks before the convention. All finalists will present at the National Convention.

Disputes[edit]

For all tests at a Convention, as well as State and Regional Competitions, if a student believes an error exists in either the question or the answer key, they can file a dispute with the dispute center, which is open usually outside the testing room for 20-30 minutes after a test has finished. Disputes will be reviewed by a team of faculty before score verifications are posted and awards are given. You can also list other members and their student ID's on a dispute form.

Disputes can cause a question to have it's answer changed, accept multiple answers, or be thrown out entirely (everyone gets the points). This only happens if the dispute is accepted.

If a dispute is filed based on a unorthodox or unique interpretation of a problem, the dispute center can choose to award only that student(s) a point (Also known as a unique dispute).

Disputes for questions on the team round are for individual parts. If more than 1 of the 4 parts for a question are thrown out, the entire question is thrown out, and the score for question 13 is used in it's place.

Awards[edit]

Individual & Minor Awards[edit]

Awards in the National Convention are as follows:

Individual: Top 20 Individuals (Top 10 Trophies)

Ciphering: Top 20 Individuals (Top 10 Trophies)

Topic Tests: Top 15 Individuals (Top 10 Trophies)

Gemini: Top 15 Pairs (Top 10 Trophies)

Interschool: Top 10 Schools

Relay: Top 15 Individuals (Top 10 Trophies)

Hustle: Top 10 Teams (All team members receive medals)

Poster: Top 10 Schools

Chalk Talk: Top 10 Individuals (Trophies)

Speed & Mental Math: Top 10 Individuals & Top 10 Sponsors (Trophies)

Major School Awards[edit]

Division Awards are calculated by adding up the Team Round score and all the composite scores (Indiv + Ciphering) of the team members in a specific division for a specific school.

The Top 10 schools receive trophies, and the individual team members receive medals.

Sweepstakes Awards are calculated by a very specific weighting formula of performances in the following tests for each school:

Individual, Ciphering, & Bowl (Top 4 Students): 36%

Topic Tests (Best Student): 45% across all tests

Interschool: 3%

Relay (Best Student in each division): 6%

Hustle: 2.5%

Poster: 1.5%

Chalk Talk (Best student in each division): 6%

The top 10 schools receive awards.

Any school that did not place in the top 15 of the sweepstakes is eligible for the Blue Ribbon Awards, which divides the sweepstakes points by the number of attending students. This promotes small schools who did very well for their size.

The top 3 schools by this formula and the aforementioned constraint receive awards.






Example Problems[edit]

Probability/Permutations/Combinations- Theta 2003

  1. 10 The set S is {#, !, @, *, $, %}. How many different proper subsets are possible?

A.6 B.63 C.64 D.127 E. NOTA

  1. 30 On a celebrity match of the Weakest Link, Big Bird and Barney make it to the final round. the final round consists of five questions per player. Play is stopped if it becomes evident that one of the contestants cannot possibly win. If Big Bird has answered his questions correctly 75% of the time and Barney has answered his questions correctly 60% of the time, what is the probability that the final round will end after each player has answered exactly four questions?

A. 3753/160000 B.2943/40000 C.3753/40000 D.3753/32000 E. NOTA

2001- Number theory Topic Test- Theta

  1. The 4-digit number 6A6B is divisible by 72. What is the sum of all possible values of A?

A. 2 B. 7 C. 9 D. 11 E. NOTA

Science Fair[edit]

At many regional and state science and engineering fairs, Mu Alpha Theta gives away prizes to high school students. These are prizes for investigating a modern mathematical problem.
